label.title: Beyond Labels: The Art of Seeing the Whole Picture
label.description: This article explores the habit of labeling and explains how oversimplified perceptions of ourselves and others prevent us from seeing true complexity. We’ll examine why labels restrict our thinking, fuel negative emotions, and damage relationships, and offer exercises to help develop a more holistic view of people and the world.

texts: Labeling is when we give ourselves or others a categorical, negative assessment based on a single event or action, without deep analysis or considering the context.
<q author="W. Somerset Maugham">People love nothing more than to label another person, freeing themselves once and for all from the need to think.</q>
For example:
• Late for a meeting — irresponsible
• Doing something for yourself — selfish
• Lying on the couch on a weekend — lazy
• Failed an exam — stupid
• Got fired — a loser
This reaction is similar to how children think: they are just learning to understand the world and try to quickly organize new information.
But as adults, we are capable of seeing the bigger picture and analyzing a situation rather than jumping to conclusions based on a single episode.
Every person is a complex, changing, and living system. Our behavior depends on age, mood, circumstances, life stages, and hundreds of other factors.
<important>Trying to describe a person with a single label is like trying to retell an entire movie with just one frame: almost everything important is left out.</important>
Labeling ourselves is especially destructive. It robs us of flexibility, prevents us from seeing our strengths, and hinders our growth.
When we label others, we risk seeing only one side of them and missing everything else that makes them human and unique.
This can lead to conflict, misunderstanding, and alienation — after all, no one likes to be boxed in.
What helps instead? Noticing facts that contradict the label and considering the different sides of a person.
For example, someone cuts in line, and your first thought is: “how rude.”
Your mood automatically drops.
But if you take a second to assume they might have an urgent reason or are having a hard day, your emotions soften and your conclusion becomes less categorical.

test.question: Which of the following statements is least consistent with the main idea of this chapter?
answers: Labeling helps us better understand people’s motives
Labels can limit our perception of others
Labels are often based on overgeneralizations and bias
Labeling can lead to misunderstanding and conflict

texts: Try these simple exercises:
“Unlabeling”

Imagine that people around you are walking around with labels on their foreheads (“failure,” “lazy,” “unattractive,” etc.). Every time you notice such a label popping up in your head, mentally strip it away.
“The Label Box”
Take a box and some sticky notes. Every time you catch yourself using a label, write it down and put it in the box. At the end of the week, throw the contents away.
You can also do this in your phone’s notes app.
“Replacing Labels”
Try replacing a negative label with a neutral or positive quality.
For example, instead of “stupid,” try “learning”; instead of “lazy,” try “exhausted, needs rest.”
This might feel unfamiliar at first, but it helps develop kindness and a more realistic perspective.
The main goal isn’t just to swap one label for another, but to gradually move away from categorical judgments and see the person, not just a single word.
The less we live through labels, the easier it becomes to notice the true complexity of ourselves and others.

lawyer.title: Technique: Become Your Own Advocate
lawyer.description: This technique offers a new way to overcome self-criticism by stepping into the role of an internal advocate. Using a courtroom analogy, you’ll learn to notice accusing thoughts, challenge them, and defend yourself with arguments based on facts and kindness. This method helps you develop a more supportive, rational, and respectful relationship with yourself.

texts: The following technique helps you work through self-criticism by encouraging you to become your own advocate. It might sound unusual, but it’s surprisingly effective.
To weaken the influence of critical thoughts, it’s important not only to notice them but also to know how to stand up to them with confidence.
The prosecutor is your inner critic, which has long been labeling you as a “failure,” “weak,” or “guilty.”
But now, you have the role of the defense attorney. Your task is to challenge the accusations and show that they are unfounded and distorted.
<q author="Elizabeth Gilbert">Be an advocate for your inner world, not a judge of your own story.</q>
Picture yourself as a competent lawyer. You won’t just say “I’m good”—you will present real facts, logical arguments, and sound explanations.
This is about managing your inner dialogue using evidence rather than emotions.
Here is an example of how this looks in practice:
<dialog psy="true">Imagine you often criticize yourself, calling yourself weak or a failure. Now, try to act as your own advocate—even if it feels difficult at first.</dialog>
<dialog psy="true">Your goal is to defend yourself honestly, logically, and respectfully, as if you were defending someone you care about deeply.</dialog>
<dialog man="true">The psychologist suggests an exercise:</dialog>
<dialog psy="true">Alright, let’s try a role-play. I’ll be the prosecutor, and you’ll be the defense attorney.</dialog>
<dialog man="true">Ready? Let’s begin.</dialog>
<dialog psy="true">(Prosecutor) Paul is weak and a failure; nothing ever works out for him.</dialog>
<dialog man="true">(Defense) That’s not true. Paul has a university degree, has achieved career success, and is surrounded by people who value him.</dialog>
<dialog psy="true">(Prosecutor) But he makes mistakes and doesn’t always cope—which means he is still a failure.</dialog>
<dialog man="true">(Defense) Making mistakes is part of being human. They don’t define a person’s entire identity or prove they are incompetent.</dialog>
<dialog psy="true">(Prosecutor) Fine. But he is weak.</dialog>
<dialog man="true">(Defense) Do you have proof? Paul works hard, makes decisions, and handles challenges. His efforts prove the opposite.</dialog>
<dialog psy="true">(Prosecutor) He could be trying harder.</dialog>
<dialog man="true">(Defense) If he truly weren’t hardworking, he wouldn’t be valued at work or considered for promotions. The claim is unfounded.</dialog>
This technique works because many people find it easier to defend others than themselves. In this case, you are learning to become an ally to yourself.
<important>As an advocate, you examine the facts, demand evidence, and refuse to let unfounded criticism sound like the truth.</important>
When negative thoughts about yourself arise, try asking: “How would I defend someone I wanted to support?”
Approach this like a professional: analyze, check the logic, and look for facts.
Here are some questions to help:
• What is the accusation? What am I being “accused” of by my thoughts?
• Is there real evidence, or is this just emotion?
• What facts support my side?
• Can I explain the situation differently, in a kinder and fairer way?
• How would a reasonable person in my position act?
• Are there external circumstances that influenced the situation?
• What can I say in my defense? What qualities and achievements can I use as arguments?

lazy.title: Awakening Your Will: Why Depression Breeds Apathy
lazy.description: This article helps you understand how depression affects motivation and the ability to take action. We explore why apathy occurs, how inactivity reinforces symptoms, and why it is vital to return to activity step by step—even when you lack the energy or desire. You will learn practical strategies to gradually regain energy, motivation, and interest in life through movement, small steps, and shifting your perspective on your own actions.

texts: During depression, starting even simple tasks can feel incredibly difficult. It often feels like motivation should come first, but it just doesn’t arrive. You might feel as if you’ve entered a “winter hibernation,” waiting for a day when everything will simply get easier on its own.
Thoughts like “nothing will bring me pleasure” or “I won’t be able to handle it anyway” can completely paralyze your ability to act.
<important>As a result, you drift further away from your usual life, friends, family, and hobbies. A sense of helplessness sets in, self-criticism grows, and your condition worsens.</important>
This creates a vicious cycle.
But it can be broken.
First, it is important to understand the nature of inactivity during depression, and then to learn techniques that can help you regain your ability to act.
One of the most insidious effects of depression is that it feels as if it “switches off” your will. Complex tasks are put off, and procrastination becomes a habitual response.
Every task feels overwhelming, motivation is absent, and you feel a strong urge to simply do nothing.
The longer this continues, the harder it becomes to take that first step. This state can drag on for weeks, months, or even years.
<q author="Fumio Sasaki">If you want to change your life, the best moment to start is the one you are in right now.</q>
Inactivity is a striking paradox of human nature.

<important>You’ve likely noticed: some people strive to live actively, try new things, and move forward. Others seem to keep their distance from life, as if they are merely observing from the sidelines.</important>
An interesting fact: if a person is isolated and deprived of their usual activities, they will almost inevitably show signs of depression after a while.
With depression, the same thing happens, but it feels voluntary and gradual—as if you are sentencing yourself to inactivity. But is this truly how you want to live?
The thought pattern during depression often looks like this:
<step title="common.event">I think about a task I could do.</step>
<step title="common.automatic">“It’s too hard / I won’t succeed / I’ll feel bad / I’m not needed by anyone.”</step>
<step title="common.emotions">Sadness, anxiety, hopelessness.</step>
<step title="common.behavior">Inactivity or procrastination.</step>
This forms a vicious cycle: negative thoughts → heavy emotions → inactivity → even less pleasure and energy → worsening depression.
Why doesn’t motivation show up?
We often assume that without desire, we can’t do anything.
But does everything in life really happen only because of motivation? Do you always go to work with enthusiasm—or sometimes simply because it’s needed?
When we say “I have no motivation,” it often means “I don’t want to” or “it’s hard to start.”
That’s normal. We don’t have to want everything that’s good for us.
In depression, almost nothing feels appealing. You want to lie down, disappear, hide. But long stretches of inaction only deepen the suffering.
The paradox is that motivation often appears after action, not before it.
Here is an example of a conversation with a psychologist about motivation:
<dialog psy="true">You used to go to the gym regularly, but now you feel no drive to do so?</dialog>
<dialog>Yes, I just don’t want to.</dialog>
<dialog psy="true">What if you imagined going to the gym without any motivation—simply because you decided to? What would happen then?</dialog>
<dialog>I would probably start feeling better even during the workout.</dialog>
<dialog psy="true">Exactly. Sometimes action creates motivation—not the other way around. You can feel tired or empty and still take a step to get a result.</dialog>
<dialog>Think of the times you did something without wanting to, but felt better afterward—that is a familiar experience.</dialog>
When we tell ourselves, “I can’t start until I feel like it,” we get stuck. But in reality, the desire often comes after the first step.
Action breeds motivation.
We’ve discussed how thoughts influence emotions, and emotions influence behavior. By shifting our thoughts, new emotions and the strength to act can emerge.
You can break out of the cycle of inactivity by gradually entering a cycle of activity and recovery.
